replies.What is your relationship with mathemati: My relationship with mathematics has always been one of fascination rather than mastery. I didn’t take it seriously until my PhD work in theoretical physics, where I needed to understand complex equations. Since then, I’ve used math as a tool for problem-solving and modeling. It’s elegant but not intuitive like the humanities.
replies.Do you ever get anxious when thinking ab: Yes, anxiety is common with me when approaching mathematical problems. My high neuroticism makes it difficult to stay calm under pressure. However, meditation from my Buddhist practice helps manage that. I often find myself second-guessing even simple calculations, which can be frustrating but also motivates me to double-check everything.
replies.Did you ever use AI to support your math: Yes, I used an AI tool for solving integrals and verifying my work on differential equations. It was helpful but not always reliable. Sometimes it gave elegant answers that were conceptually off. I had to verify them with more fundamental methods, which taught me to be skeptical of any solution, even one generated by a machine.
replies.How would you explain, step by step, how: First, write the standard form: ay'' + by' + cy = 0. Assume solutions of exponential type, then substitute and obtain a characteristic equation. Solve that quadratic for roots r1 and r2. If they are real and distinct, use y = C1e^(r1x) + C2e^(r2x). If complex conjugates, use e^(αx)(C1cos(βx)+C2sin(βx)).

To find stationary points, differentiate f(x) and set f'(x)=0. Solve for x to get critical values. Then use the second derivative test: if f''(x)>0 at that point it is a local minimum; if <0 then a maximum; if zero, inconclusive. Plotting or using a graphing tool helps visualize these points.

First center the data, then compute the covariance matrix and find eigenvalues/eigenvectors. Sort eigenvectors by decreasing eigenvalue; project original data onto these axes.
